 1                          I.    INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.   My name is Justin Bieber. My business address is 111 East Broadway, Suite 1200, Salt

 4        Lake City, Utah, 84111.

 5   Q.   ARE YOU THE SAME JUSTIN BIEBER WHO PREVIOUSLY FILED DIRECT

 6        TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING ON BEHALF OF THE NEW MEXICO

 7        LARGE CUSTOMER GROUP (“NMLCG”)?

 8   A.   Yes, I am.

 9   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR STIPULATION TESTIMONY?

10   A.   My stipulation testimony recommends approval of the Comprehensive Stipulation

11        Agreement (“Stipulation”) of Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS” or

12        “Company”), New Mexico Department of Justice (“NMDOJ”), the NMLCG, Occidental

13        Permian Ltd. (“OPL”), Louisiana Energy Services L.L.C. (“LES”), Federal Executive

14        Agencies (“FEA”), Targa Resources Corp. (“Targa”), Walmart Inc. (“Walmart”), Coalition

15        for Clean Affordable Energy (“CCAE”), and Prosperity Works (collectively, the

16        “Signatories”). In particular, I testify on behalf of the NMLCG in support of the revenue

17        allocation incorporated into the Stipulation. NMLCG witness Celia B. Hashlamoun

18        testifies in support of the stipulated revenue requirement incorporated into the Stipulation.




                                                   1
                                            Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                   Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1                           II.    COMPREHENSIVE STIPULATION

 2   Q.     HOW DOES THE COMPREHENSIVE STIPULATION ADDRESS REVENUE

 3          REQUIREMENT ISSUES.

 4   A.     The Signatories1 to the Stipulation agree that the Company should be authorized to

 5          implement an increase in New Mexico retail base rate revenues of $90,000,000, effective

 6          December 1, 2026.2 The Stipulation identifies a return on equity (“ROE”) of 9.5% and

 7          several cost-of-service components, including capital structure, SPS’s working capital

 8          balance, and depreciation rates.3

 9                  Except as specifically noted above, the stipulated base rate revenue increase is not

10          associated with any specific calculation involving any of the stated cost of service

11          components, or approval or disapproval of any other issue raised in this case. The

12          Signatories arrived at the stipulated base rate revenue increase through a compromise of

13          the various issues raised in this case without specifically accepting or rejecting for purposes

14          of this Stipulation any ratemaking issue or principle other than those specified.4




     1
       The Signatories are: SPS, NMDOJ, NMLCG, OPL, LES, FEA, Targa, Walmart, CCAE, and Prosperity Works.
     Commission Staff does not oppose parts of the Stipulation.

     3

     4

                                         Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1   Q.         DO THE SETTLING PARTIES AGREE ON ANY PARTICULAR COST OF

 2              SERVICE METHODOLOGIES?

 3   A.         Yes. The Signatories agree that SPS shall allocate all costs of production and transmission,

 4              including Hale and Sagamore wind generation, on an average-and-excess demand four-

 5              coincident-peak (“AED 4-CP”) basis. And the Stipulation specifies that the load factor

 6              used in the AED 4-CP method uses the system single peak demand for the year (“1CP”).5

 7   Q.         DOES THE STIPULATION INCLUDE AN UPDATED CLASS COST OF

 8              SERVICE STUDY (“CCOSS”) THAT REFLECTS THE TERMS OF THE

 9              STIPULATION?

10   A.         No. The Stipulation does not include an updated CCOSS reflecting the settled revenue

11              requirement or the agreed-upon cost allocation methodologies.

12                      However, in his direct testimony, OPL witness Jonathan Ly provided an alternative

13              CCOSS that incorporates the two cost allocation methodology changes ultimately reflected

14              in the Stipulation: (1) allocating the Hale and Sagamore Wind Projects using the AED-4CP

15              methodology, and (2) using the system 1 CP to calculate the system load factor.6 Although

16              Mr. Ly’s study was developed using the Company’s filed revenue requirement and does

17              not reflect all terms of the Stipulation, it provides a useful indication of the direction in




     5
         Id. at p. 9.
     6
         Direct Testimony and Exhibits of Jonathan Ly, Exhibit JL-5 (May 1, 2026).


                                                               3
                                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                           Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1              which the agreed-upon cost allocation methodology changes would affect the allocation of

 2              costs among customer classes.

 3                        Specifically, Mr. Ly’s alternative CCOSS results showed higher allocated costs of

 4              service for the Residential, Small General, Secondary General, Municipal & School, and

 5              Irrigation rate schedules relative to the Company’s original CCOSS. Conversely, the

 6              results showed lower allocated costs of service for the Primary General and Large General

 7              Service Transmission (“LGS-T”) rate schedules, with relatively minor differences in the

 8              allocated cost of service for the lighting rate schedules. 7

 9   Q.         HOW DOES THE STIPULATION ADDRESS REVENUE ALLOCATION?

10   A.         Notwithstanding the agreement on the CCOSS methodologies, the Signatories agree on a

11              stipulated base rate revenue allocation that departs from the CCOSS results in favor of

12              gradual rate changes for various customer classes. Table JB-1 below summarizes the

13              agreed upon class revenue allocation.

4   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW THE STIPULATED REVENUE ALLOCATION

5        COMPARES TO COST CAUSATION?

6   A.   As I explained above, the Stipulation does not include an updated CCOSS that reflects the

7        stipulated revenue requirement and cost allocation methodologies.                  However, it is

                                   Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

2      from its filed case. These results are summarized in Table JB-2 below.

6                In the table above, the second column presents the cost-based base rate increase

7      identified in SPS’s filed CCOSS. The third column expresses the cost-based increase



                                                            6
                                         Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1        relative to the system average. The fourth column presents the stipulated base rate increase,

 2        while the fifth column expresses the stipulated increase relative to the system average.

 3               Because the cost allocation results and the stipulated revenue allocation are based

 4        on different overall revenue requirements, directly comparing the percentage rate increases

 5        can be misleading. Expressing each class’s increase relative to the system average

 6        normalizes the results and provides a meaningful basis for comparison to illustrate how

 7        each customer class is treated under the Company’s filed CCOSS relative to the Stipulation

 8        despite the differences in the underlying revenue requirements.

 9   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW THE STIPULATED REVENUE ALLOCATION

10        BALANCES ALIGNMENT WITH COST CAUSATION AND GRADUALISM?

11   A.   The stipulated revenue allocation moves all classes closer to cost of service while also

12        reflecting gradualism. Each class that required an above-average cost-based rate increase

13        receives an above-average base rate increase under the Stipulation. Specifically, the

14        Residential, Small General, Secondary General, Municipal & School, and lighting classes

15        all required an above-average cost-based rate increase and received an above-average

16        stipulated rate increase. Conversely, the Irrigation, Primary General, and LGS-T classes

17        required a below-average cost-based increase and received below-average stipulated

18        increases.




                                                    7
                                         Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1               At the same time, the Stipulation moderates the movement toward cost of service.

 2        All rate schedules except Irrigation, Primary General, and LGS-T received stipulated

 3        increases that were substantially below their cost-based increases on a relative basis. For

 4        example, Residential customers required a cost-based rate increase equal to 237.7% of the

 5        system average, but received a stipulated increase equal to only 139.5% of the system

 6        average. Similarly, Small General required a cost-based increase equal to 260.0% of the

 7        system average, but received a stipulated increase equal to only 139.5% of the system

 8        average. Secondary General required a cost-based increase equal to 166.6% of the system

 9        average but received a stipulated increase equal to only 135.7% of the system average. The

10        subsidies required to moderate the rate impacts for these rate schedules were funded by the

11        Irrigation, Primary General, and LGS-T rate schedules.

12               This approach balances cost causation and gradualism by moving each class in the

13        direction indicated by the cost-of-service results, while limiting the magnitude of the

14        increases for classes that would otherwise receive substantially larger cost-based increases.

15   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE COMPARISON OF THE STIPULATED

16        REVENUE ALLOCATION TO THE COMPANY’S CCOSS RESULTS SHOULD

17        BE VIEWED CONSERVATIVELY?

18   A.   As I explained above, the Stipulation does not include an updated CCOSS reflecting either

19        the stipulated revenue requirement or the agreed-upon cost allocation methodologies.




                                                   8
                                    Case No. 25-00079-UT
                           Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1   Nevertheless, comparing the stipulated revenue allocation to the Company’s filed CCOSS

 2   remains informative. However, that comparison should be viewed conservatively because

 3   the agreed-upon CCOSS methodology modifications would increase the cost-based

 4   revenue responsibility for the customer classes that receive the greatest degree of revenue

 5   allocation moderation under the Stipulation.

 6          Specifically, as discussed above, the alternative CCOSS study sponsored by Mr.

 7   Ly—which incorporated the stipulated cost allocation methodologies—showed even

 8   higher allocated costs of service for the Residential, Small General, Secondary General,

 9   Municipal & School, and Irrigation rate schedules than the Company’s original CCOSS.

10   Conversely, it indicated lower allocated costs of service for the Primary General and LGS-

11   T rate schedules, while the lighting rate schedules experienced only relatively minor

12   decreases.

13          Residential customers provide a useful example. Under the Company’s original

14   CCOSS, the Residential class required a cost-based base rate increase equal to

15   approximately 237.7% of the system average but received a stipulated increase equal to

16   only 139.5% of the system average. The alternative CCOSS studies indicate that applying

17   the stipulated cost allocation methodologies would increase the Residential class’s

18   allocated cost of service even further. As a result, if an updated CCOSS had been prepared

19   using the stipulated methodologies, the Residential class would have required an even




                                              9
                                          Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                 Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1        larger cost-based increase than shown in the Company’s filed study, while its stipulated

 2        increase would remain unchanged. Accordingly, the degree of moderation, or subsidy,

 3        provided to the Residential class under the Stipulation is actually greater than reflected by

 4        the comparison to the Company’s original CCOSS.

 5                The same principle applies to the Small General, Secondary General, and Municipal

 6        & School rate schedules. Consequently, comparing the stipulated revenue allocation to the

 7        Company’s original filed CCOSS understates the extent to which the Stipulation moderates

 8        rate increases for those customer classes relative to cost of service and should be viewed

 9        conservatively.

10   Q.   WHAT WAS THE EXTENT OF THE NMLCG’S PARTICIPATION IN THE

11        SETTLEMENT PROCESS?

12   A.   NMLCG counsel and expert witnesses participated in settlement negotiations among the

13        settlement parties. As an expert witness, I reviewed settlement proposals, terms, and

14        supporting documents that were circulated between the parties.

15   Q.   IS THE STIPULATION THE PRODUCT OF SERIOUS BARGAINING AMONG

16        CAPABLE, KNOWLEDGEABLE PARTIES?

17   A.   Yes, the settling parties represent a wide variety of diverse interests, including the interests

18        of the utility, residential and low-income customers, commercial customers, and industrial

19        customers. The settling parties have extensive experience in ratemaking matters and are




                                                    10
                                         Case No. 25-00079-UT
                                Stipulation Testimony of Justin Bieber

 1        represented by competent counsel. Moreover, the parties had ample time to review and

 2        analyze the record prior to settlement.

 3   Q.   DOES THE STIPULATION, AS A PACKAGE, BENEFIT CUSTOMERS AND THE

 4        PUBLIC INTEREST?

 5   A.   Yes. The Stipulation resolves matters related to the revenue requirement and allocation of

 6        revenues for electric service in a balanced way that adheres to principles of gradualism and

 7        benefits both SPS and its customers.

 8   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN WHY THE STIPULATED ALLOCATION OF ELECTRIC

 9        REVENUES BETWEEN CUSTOMER CLASSES IS IN THE PUBLIC INTEREST?

10   A.   The stipulated class allocation of electric revenues represents a compromise that takes into

11        account the various positions among the parties in the case on this issue. As I explained

12        above, the agreed upon allocation of electric revenues among customer classes represents

13        a compromise between parties’ positions that reflect the underlying cost of service while

14        also adhering to the principle of gradualism. Based on the circumstances of this case, and

15        in consideration of the record regarding the allocation of electric revenues between

16        customers classes, the stipulated revenue allocation is reasonable and in the public interest.

17        I respectfully recommend the Commission approve the Stipulation in its entirety.

18   Q.   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR SETTLEMENT TESTIMONY?

19   A.   Yes, it does.
